books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10: Dr. Francis Townsend of California proposed an Old Age Revolving Pension Plan. Every American over 60 would receive 200 dollars a month, paid for by a national sales tax, on one condition: the pensioner had to spend the whole 200 dollars within the month. Townsend argued that this flood of spending by older Americans would revive production and end the Depression, while also ending poverty among the elderly.

stem: Roosevelt answered the Townsend, Long, and Coughlin movements mainly by

options.text: Taking up their pension demand in his own program
Banning all their radio broadcasts at once
options.misconception: Coughlin was ordered off the air only in 1942, and Townsend and Long were never banned; Roosevelt answered them politically, not by silencing them.

options.text: Adopting the Liberty League's demand for lower taxes
options.misconception: Lower taxes were the Liberty League's demand on the right, not the answer Roosevelt gave to critics on the left.

options.text: Ignoring them as too small to matter at all
options.misconception: Roosevelt treated these movements as a serious political threat, and the Townsend plan helped spur the Social Security Act.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the books say the Townsend plan helped spur Roosevelt to develop the Social Security Act, taking the pension demand into his own program.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Coughlin kept broadcasting until 1942, so Roosevelt did not answer these movements by banning them.
rationales.C: Background from the books: lower taxes belonged to the Liberty League on the right; Roosevelt answered the left by offering pensions, not tax cuts.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Roosevelt took these movements seriously enough to shape the Second New Deal around their demands.
rationales.general:
1. Townsend, Long, and Coughlin all said Roosevelt was doing too little for ordinary people.
2. Each drew a large following that could pull voters away from Roosevelt.
3. The books say the Townsend plan helped spur the Social Security Act.
4. So Roosevelt answered a rival demand by adopting part of it himself.
Remember: a president can defeat a rival idea by putting a version of it into law.
